title: How LLMs Generate: Tokens & the Context Window

scenes.heading: How LLMs Generate: Tokens & the Context Window
scenes.narration: Let's look at how models actually read and write text, and why the context window shapes everything an agent can do.

scenes.heading: Tokens, not words
items: Models process text as tokens, not whole words
Common words are one token; rare ones split
Rough rule: about four characters per token
scenes.narration: First, models don't read words or characters. They read tokens, which are sub-word chunks. A common word is often a single token, while a rare word, a chunk of code, or punctuation splits into several. A handy rule of thumb for English is about four characters per token. Everything about limits and cost is measured in tokens, so it pays to think in them.

scenes.heading: Everything shares one budget
steps: System prompt claims part of the window
The answer needs room reserved too
scenes.narration: The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can see in one call, and it's a single shared budget. The system prompt takes a slice. Your tool schemas take another. The running conversation grows every turn, retrieved documents add more, and you still have to reserve space for the answer itself. Grow one and you shrink another, which is why agents feel this pressure constantly.

scenes.code:
WINDOW = 128_000                    # model-specific ceiling
RESERVED_FOR_ANSWER = 2_000

def est_tokens(text: str) -> int:
    return max(1, len(text) // 4)   # ~4 chars per token

used = est_tokens(system) + est_tokens(tools) + est_tokens(history)
budget_left = WINDOW - used - RESERVED_FOR_ANSWER
assert budget_left > 0, "trim or summarise history before calling"
scenes.heading: Budgeting the window
scenes.narration: Here's that budget as code. We set the window to the model's ceiling and reserve a couple thousand tokens for the answer. Our estimate function divides characters by four to approximate tokens. Then we add up the system prompt, tool schemas, and history, subtract the reservation, and assert there's room left. When history outgrows the budget, the call fails, so you must trim or summarise before you overflow.

scenes.text: Tokens drive both cost and latency; the context window is the hard ceiling every agent lives inside.
scenes.narration: The takeaway: input and output share one hard ceiling, and tokens drive both what you pay and how long you wait. An agent that resends a huge history on every loop is slow and expensive. That's exactly why counting tokens underpins summarization, memory, and every optimization that comes later.
